newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Philharmonic leader says won't play with women.
newsitem.headline: Philharmonic leader says won't play with women.

text.p: The director of the Vienna Philharmonic said on Thursday he would rather disband Austria's most prestigious orchestra than bow to pressure to admit women.
"This is a private club and we won't have our arm twisted. If people keep trying to pressure us (into admitting women), we'll dissolve ourselves," Werner Resel told state radio.
He said the orchestra, which has resolutely refused to allow women to play in its ranks, had received threatening letters, mainly from the United States.
"Women in America are certainly getting their information from Austria...This is typical Austrian masochism," Resel said.
The Vienna Philharmonic, technically a private club, is under no obligation to vote on admitting women.
Founded in 1842 and famous for its annual New Year's concert, it starts an international tour later this month and is due to play in the United States in March.
It has braced itself for boycotts and an onslaught of protests from U.S. women's groups.
Austrian politicians, including Chancellor Viktor Klima, have also urged the Philharmonic to end its men-only policy and "use the creative potential of the other half of humanity".
The opposition Greens slammed Resel's comments and said the orchestra should be forced to repay government subsidies.

"The Philharmoniker has never had any qualms about taking money from women taxpayers," Greens parliamentary leader Madeleine Petrovic said. "This men's club must have a deep-seated fear of female competition."

The Philharmonic's sister orchestra at the State Opera has also dealt a severe blow to Resel. The opera orchestra, which contains many Philharmonic musicians, announced on Wednesday it would soon begin auditioning women.
A meeting on February 27 will clear up details such as maternity payments ahead of a formal vote. The Philharmonic leaves on tour the following day.
"Of course we are opposed to sex discrimination," State Opera director Ioan Holender said.

Resel remained unbowed, however. "Under Austrian health and safety rules there could be times when the orchestra would be unable to play," he said, raising the spectre of an orchestra paralysed by mass pregnancy.
